title: Google Earth Now Lets You Add AI Images — But Experts Say It Could Cause Big Problems
summary: Have you ever zoomed in on your house in Google Earth? Now imagine you could type 'flood' and watch the streets fill with water — even if it's sunny outside. That's what Google's new AI feature does. You just type what you want to see, and it paints it onto the satellite view. But experts who use satellite images to check facts are really worried. NPR tested it and easily made fake pictures of Iran's Kharg Island on fire and the U.S. Capitol underwater. Neither event happened, but if someone shared those images, they could fool a lot of people. 'Satellite imagery has been kind of a safe bet when it comes to verifying an event because it's hard to fake,' says Jake Godin from Bellingcat, a group that investigates news using photos and videos. Now, with a few clicks, anyone can create a convincing fake. Henk van Ess, a researcher, tried making 'refugees at the Mexican border, a nuclear plant in Iran, a crash in Amsterdam, a hospital with a bomb crater in Gaza.' Google's tool didn't refuse any of them. This worries journalists and investigators because Google Earth is often used to check if something posted online is real. 'The fake is made inside the thing people use to check whether pictures are true,' van Ess said. Google says the feature is for imagination, but many think it could make misinformation spread even faster. And if governments start saying real satellite images are fake, it could get even harder to know what's true.
why_it_matters: If you cannot trust the pictures you see online, it becomes harder to know which news stories are real, affecting how you understand the world around you.

background_read: Satellite images have long been used by journalists and aid groups to see what is happening in faraway places during wars or disasters.
The U.S. Capitol (the building where Congress meets) and Kharg Island (a major oil-shipping island in Iran) are real locations often shown in satellite pictures.
In recent years, AI tools that create fake but realistic images have become very easy to use, making it harder for people to tell what is real online.
Article_Structure: WHO: Google and its new AI tool, along with fact-checking experts like Jake Godin and Henk van Ess.
WHAT: Google Earth now lets users add AI-generated scenes onto satellite images, which worry experts about fake news.
WHERE: On Google Earth's platform, with test fakes of places like Iran's Kharg Island and the U.S. Capitol.
WHY: Because convincing fake satellite pictures could make people believe events that never happened and spread misinformation faster.

perspectives.description: Google says the feature is meant for imagination and fun, letting people see hypothetical "what if" scenes.
Fact-checkers worry that anyone can now create realistic fakes inside a trusted tool, making it much harder to stop false information from spreading.
